--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Comparison.column_summary()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Pointblank description: Get a per-column summary of value mismatches. twitter-card: title: >- [Comparison.column_summary()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Pointblank description: Get a per-column summary of value mismatches. title: >- [Comparison.column_summary()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Get a per-column summary of value mismatches. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get a per-column summary of value mismatches. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/blob/main/pointblank/_compare.py#L2173-L2263){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Comparison.column_summary() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} A row counts as `"changed"` if any compared column differs, so the row statuses don't say which columns are responsible. `column_summary()` does. It's often the quickest way to find the cause of a difference. A single column with mismatches in every row suggests a change in how that column is computed or formatted, while mismatches spread thinly across many columns suggest changed rows. The summary also lists each column's data type on both sides and the target column it was compared against, which shows the effect of `column_map=`. The counts are computed when the comparison is made, so this doesn't query the tables again. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A table (Polars if available, else Pandas) with one row per compared column: the source and target column names and data types, the number of matched rows whose values differ (`n_mismatch`), and that number as a fraction of matched rows (`f_mismatch`). Matched rows are those with a status of `"match"` or `"changed"`. In multiset mode, there are no matched pairs, so the last two columns are null. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Here, a rewritten job produces an orders table where the totals are rounded to whole units, and one order has a different status. ::: {#035cef8b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pointblank as pb import polars as pl orders_old = pl.DataFrame( { "order_id": [1, 2, 3, 4], "status": ["shipped", "shipped", "pending", "shipped"], "total": [19.99, 45.50, 12.00, 80.25], } ) orders_new = pl.DataFrame( { "order_id": [1, 2, 3, 4], "status": ["shipped", "shipped", "cancelled", "shipped"], "total": [20.0, 46.0, 12.0, 80.0], } ) comparison = pb.compare(orders_old, orders_new, keys="order_id") comparison.column_summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

All four rows are `"changed"`, but the summary separates the two causes. Once the rounding is accepted (for instance, with `tolerance={"total": 0.5}`), only the status change is left.
